performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet, conductor
intro: A procession of muted trumpets approaches through the quick violin figures of Fêtes. For a few bars the two fill the orchestra together; at the end, only a distant drum and the low strings keep moving.

sections.label: A · Quick violins, high flutes
sections.mNote: Triplet figures circulate through strings and winds

sections.label: B · The muted-trumpet procession
sections.mNote: A♭ and E♭ in the bass support the approaching march

sections.label: B′ · Brass march, dancing strings
sections.mNote: The procession’s broad tune meets the quick violin figures

sections.label: A′ · Flutes lead the dance again
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns with flowing winds and quick cellos

sections.label: Coda · The procession recedes
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases leave the drum and low strings behind

cues.title: Violins under high flutes
cues.text: The violins begin with quick repeated triplets, sharply accented. High flutes hold above them. Cor anglais and clarinets soon join the dance, sending an upward phrase across the string rhythm.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, Kalmus reprint, printed p. 19: opening violin triplets and held flutes, then cor anglais and clarinets. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A procession through the festival
cues.text: Debussy’s programme puts a fantastic procession inside the festivities. It approaches, passes through the crowd and merges with the dance. His orchestra has to keep the marching band and the dancers going at once.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s introductory programme for Nocturnes, reproduced by the Los Angeles Philharmonic: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes

cues.title: A distant tread
cues.text: A♭ and E♭ repeat in the bass, with very soft timpani and harp. The metre changes to 2/4. Muted trumpets bring the procession’s broad tune over this steady tread, still far away.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 10, printed pp. 43–44: Modéré mais toujours très rythmé, 2/4, A♭–E♭ accompaniment and muted trumpets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The two crowds meet
cues.text: The trumpet tune now has trombones beneath it. Fast violin figures and little woodwind bursts surround the march, with snare drum and cymbals joining in. Debussy asks the brass for a full tone without harshness.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 13, printed p. 48: combined brass melody and quick strings, woodwind figures, snare drum and cymbals; the brass instruction asks for a ringing tone without harshness.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flutes after the march
cues.text: The first tempo returns in 6/8. Flutes run above short reed phrases and a quick cello pulse. The heavy brass falls silent, leaving the dance on its feet again.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 14, printed p. 53: 1er tempo, 6/8, flute and reed phrases, repeated cello notes, then rests in the brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chevillard’s first two nocturnes
cues.text: At the first performance in Paris on 9 December 1900, Camille Chevillard conducts just Nuages and Fêtes. Sirènes, with its wordless women’s chorus, joins them at the complete première the following October.
cues.evidence: Premières on 9 December 1900 and 27 October 1901, conducted by Chevillard: https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes_(Debussy,_Claude). The scoring and chronology are also given at https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes.

cues.title: The drum keeps going
cues.text: The wind players finish their last fragments. A snare drum continues very softly, with cellos and basses playing at the tip of the bow. Debussy asks the low strings to move ever farther away. The festival disappears while its feet are still moving.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, printed p. 70: snare drum ppp, cellos and basses du bout de l’archet, pp et toujours en s’éloignant davantage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A♭ and E♭ begin the march
transitions.how: Modéré mais toujours très rythmé: moderate, still strongly rhythmic. The dance contracts to quiet harp, timpani and plucked basses, with A♭ and E♭ repeating in 2/4. Cellos join the tread, then muted trumpets unfold the procession’s tune above it.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 10, printed pp. 43–44. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336

transitions.title: The dance surrounds the march
transitions.how: The marching bass continues as trumpets and trombones broaden the tune. Above them, quick violin figures and woodwind triplets bring back the dance. Snare drum and cymbals join the crescendo. The brass marking asks for a full, ringing tone without harshness.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 13, printed p. 48: broad brass tune against fast strings and winds, with percussion.

transitions.title: The flutes take over
transitions.to: A′ · Flutes lead the dance again
transitions.how: At 1er tempo, 6/8 replaces the procession’s 2/4. The brass and percussion stop after the first chord, and flutes carry a running line above short reed figures. Repeated cello notes keep the bass moving beneath this lighter dance.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 14, printed p. 53: first tempo, 6/8 and the handover to winds and cellos.

transitions.title: The procession moves away
transitions.from: A′ · Flutes lead the dance again
transitions.how: The late dance breaks into short wind phrases and quieter brass replies. Low-string figures keep running as the other players fall silent. In the final bars the snare drum returns at ppp, beside cellos and basses playing lightly at the tip of the bow.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, closing pages, especially printed pp. 69–70. The established coda boundary locates the retreat as a whole.

source.title: Debussy, Nocturnes, original orchestral score, Kalmus reprint of Fromont
source.locator: Fêtes, printed pp. 19–70: quick violins and held flutes at the opening, the procession at rehearsal 10, its meeting with the dance at rehearsal 13, and the final snare-drum and low-string phrases.

timeline.note: The violins run in quick groups of three beneath high, held flute notes.
Reeds dart upwards through the string figures; horns and trumpets add short calls.
Upper winds trade quick figures above moving strings and held horn notes.
Winds and strings exchange short phrases, with timpani marking the bass notes underneath.
Harps, timpani and low strings start the procession with quiet, repeated steps.
Muted trumpets sing the procession tune above the repeated low notes.
Woodwind replies and horns join the procession as the strings begin to move more quickly.
The brass procession meets the dancing strings, with high wind calls, both harps and percussion.
Flutes and oboes recover the quick dance above the cellos’ pulse; the brass falls silent.
Piccolo and flutes rise above the moving strings, with horns and timpani underneath.
Soft brass remembers the procession while the low strings keep its repeated steps going.
Brief woodwind phrases pass above soft low brass and plucked string chords.
Snare drum, cellos and basses continue quietly, the strings playing at the tips of their bows.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande (orchestra), Ernest Ansermet (conductor)
fields.note: The instrumental movement has no choral part. No orchestral soloist or complete roster is identified or inferred. The unresolved Sirènes chorus does not enter this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original orchestral work; exact performing edition unestablished
fields.note: The sources identify the work and movement, but not the parts or revision used in October 1951. The original Fromont/Kalmus and 1930 Jobert full scores were viewed. Musical annotations use shared principal passages; no claim that Ansermet follows every detail of the revised edition, no cut/repeat-order certification, and no bar-accurate score alignment. Orchestra states are explicitly provisional passage estimates, not audio instrument detection.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Month and year are corroborated. Stuart’s [a] Nocturnes has no exact day: the 10th and 12th in the shared session heading refer to other works. The 1951 session must not be described as a 1951 publication.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue is independently supplied by the session discography and the matching London CD catalogue record.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original British LP label; London LL 530 is the separately dated June 1952 issue in Stuart.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: First British issue March 1952. Side A contains the three Nocturnes; side B Ravel’s Rapsodie espagnole. Original label images were not present in the IA item, so the date relies on the discography rather than an inspected LP label.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side A; suite master series SAR587–SAR592
fields.note: IA identifies the side and track order; Stuart assigns SAR587–92 to Nocturnes as a whole. No individual movement matrix, LP runout, take number or pressing identification is established, and none is extrapolated from the six-number series.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No digital-transfer engineer is credited. IA account identity is not a transfer credit. Victor Olof (producer) and Gil Went (engineer) are documented for the original Decca session, not for this digital transfer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded/published on IA on 26 December 2021. That is not evidence for when the physical record was transferred.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original FLAC and derived VBR MP3 are listed, but playback equipment, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, pitch correction and intervening edits are undocumented. No listening or processing-quality claim is made.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public-domain underlying composition under ordinary life-plus-70 terms
fields.note: Debussy died in 1918; the original score was published in 1900–01. Original and 1930 score pages were consulted as historical score evidence. This assessment of the composition is separate from sound-recording rights and does not claim rights in a modern edition, scan or arrangement.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 territorial basis: EU sound recording first published before 1963; US public-domain status not established
fields.note: LXT 2637 was issued in March 1952, not 1951. Under the ordinary former EU 50-year publication term this predates expiry before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. This is the project’s territorial pre-1963 basis, not a Creative Commons licence or a worldwide public-domain claim. US status has not been established. IA supplies no open-licence URL; the upload alone does not grant rights.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
